scene.label: Act 3, Scene 2
scene.title: SCENE II. A street in Windsor

lines.text: Nay, keep your way, little gallant. You were wont to be a follower, but now you are a leader. Whether had you rather, lead mine eyes, or eye your master's heels?
lines.plainText: Nay keep your way little gallant You were wont to be a follower but now you are a leader Whether had you rather lead mine eyes or eye your master's heels

lines.text: I had rather, forsooth, go before you like a man than follow him like a dwarf.
lines.plainText: I had rather forsooth go before you like a man than follow him like a dwarf

lines.text: O, you are a flattering boy! Now I see you'll be a courtier.
lines.plainText: O you are a flattering boy Now I see you'll be a courtier

lines.text: Well met, Mistress Page. Whither go you?
lines.plainText: Well met Mistress Page Whither go you

lines.text: Truly, sir, to see your wife. Is she at home?
lines.plainText: Truly sir to see your wife Is she at home

lines.text: Ay, and as idle as she may hang together, for want of company. I think if your husbands were dead you two would marry.
lines.plainText: Ay and as idle as she may hang together for want of company I think if your husbands were dead you two would marry

lines.text: Be sure of that—two other husbands.
lines.plainText: Be sure of thattwo other husbands

lines.text: Where had you this pretty weathercock?
lines.plainText: Where had you this pretty weathercock

lines.text: I cannot tell what the dickens his name is my husband had him of. What do you call your knight's name, sirrah?
lines.plainText: I cannot tell what the dickens his name is my husband had him of What do you call your knight's name sirrah

lines.text: Sir John Falstaff.
lines.plainText: Sir John Falstaff

lines.text: Sir John Falstaff!
lines.plainText: Sir John Falstaff

lines.text: He, he; I can never hit on's name. There is such a league between my good man and he! Is your wife at home indeed?
lines.plainText: He he I can never hit on's name There is such a league between my good man and he Is your wife at home indeed

lines.text: Indeed she is.
lines.plainText: Indeed she is

lines.text: By your leave, sir, I am sick till I see her.
lines.plainText: By your leave sir I am sick till I see her

lines.text: Has Page any brains? Hath he any eyes? Hath he any thinking? Sure, they sleep; he hath no use of them. Why, this boy will carry a letter twenty mile as easy as a cannon will shoot point-blank twelve score. He pieces out his wife's inclination, he gives her folly motion and advantage. And now she's going to my wife, and Falstaff's boy with her. A man may hear this shower sing in the wind. And Falstaff's boy with her! Good plots they are laid, and our revolted wives share damnation together. Well, I will take him, then torture my wife, pluck the borrowed veil of modesty from the so-seeming Mistress Page, divulge Page himself for a secure and wilful Actaeon, and to these violent proceedings all my neighbours shall cry aim. [Clock strikes.] The clock gives me my cue, and my assurance bids me search. There I shall find Falstaff. I shall be rather praised for this than mocked, for it is as positive as the earth is firm that Falstaff is there. I will go.

content.text: Enter Page, Shallow, Slender, Host, Sir Hugh Evans, Caius and Rugby.

lines.text: Trust me, a good knot. I have good cheer at home, and I pray you all go with me.
lines.plainText: Trust me a good knot I have good cheer at home and I pray you all go with me

lines.text: I must excuse myself, Master Ford.
lines.plainText: I must excuse myself Master Ford

lines.text: And so must I, sir; we have appointed to dine with Mistress Anne, and I would not break with her for more money than I'll speak of.
lines.plainText: And so must I sir we have appointed to dine with Mistress Anne and I would not break with her for more money than I'll speak of

lines.text: We have lingered about a match between Anne Page and my cousin Slender, and this day we shall have our answer.
lines.plainText: We have lingered about a match between Anne Page and my cousin Slender and this day we shall have our answer

lines.text: I hope I have your good will, father Page.
lines.plainText: I hope I have your good will father Page

lines.text: You have, Master Slender, I stand wholly for you.—But my wife, Master doctor, is for you altogether.
lines.plainText: You have Master Slender I stand wholly for youBut my wife Master doctor is for you altogether

lines.text: Ay, be-gar; and de maid is love-a me! My nursh-a Quickly tell me so mush.
lines.plainText: Ay begar and de maid is lovea me My nursha Quickly tell me so mush

lines.text: What say you to young Master Fenton? He capers, he dances, he has eyes of youth, he writes verses, he speaks holiday, he smells April and May. He will carry 't, he will carry 't. 'Tis in his buttons he will carry 't.
lines.plainText: What say you to young Master Fenton He capers he dances he has eyes of youth he writes verses he speaks holiday he smells April and May He will carry 't he will carry 't 'Tis in his buttons he will carry 't

lines.text: Not by my consent, I promise you. The gentleman is of no having. He kept company with the wild Prince and Poins. He is of too high a region, he knows too much. No, he shall not knit a knot in his fortunes with the finger of my substance. If he take her, let him take her simply. The wealth I have waits on my consent, and my consent goes not that way.

lines.text: I beseech you, heartily, some of you go home with me to dinner. Besides your cheer, you shall have sport: I will show you a monster. Master Doctor, you shall go; so shall you, Master Page, and you, Sir Hugh.
lines.plainText: I beseech you heartily some of you go home with me to dinner Besides your cheer you shall have sport I will show you a monster Master Doctor you shall go so shall you Master Page and you Sir Hugh

lines.text: Well, fare you well. We shall have the freer wooing at Master Page's.
lines.plainText: Well fare you well We shall have the freer wooing at Master Page's

lines.text: Go home, John Rugby; I come anon.
lines.plainText: Go home John Rugby I come anon

lines.text: Farewell, my hearts. I will to my honest knight Falstaff, and drink canary with him.
lines.plainText: Farewell my hearts I will to my honest knight Falstaff and drink canary with him

lines.text: [Aside.] I think I shall drink in pipe-wine first with him; I'll make him dance.—Will you go, gentles?
lines.plainText: Aside I think I shall drink in pipewine first with him I'll make him danceWill you go gentles

lines.text: Have with you to see this monster.
